newsitem.title: ITALY: U.S. rejects 'rhetoric and emotion' in soya row.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rejects 'rhetoric and emotion' in soya row.

text.p: The U.S. government, rejecting an environmentalist charge that is in the lap of big business, urged consumers on Thursday not to be swayed by "rhetoric and emotion" in a row about genetically altered soybeans.
Acknowledging European mistrust of the beans developed in the United States, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman reminded consumers that most cancer drugs were based on similar science.

"It is an issue that is very easily whipped up with rhetoric and emotion, and it is incumbent on all leaders to educate people on what the facts are and make sure science is objective," Glickman told reporters during a U.N. food summit.
"Saying that does not mean we have all the answers or that in a supine or blind way we follow industry," he said.
Glickman, who was the target of a nude protest about the beans at the summit on Wednesday, was speaking as campaigners tried unsuccessfully to stage a new coup in Rome on Friday.
A group of about 20 teenagers tried to invade the Rome office of Anglo-Dutch food firm Unilever but the action turned out to be a flop when they could not get in, reporters said.
The environmental group Greenpeace said at the summit on Thursday that genetic engineering was no answer to world food problems and urged a moratorium on the sale of genetically modified products.
In the United States, seventeen people from the same group were arrested later that day for disrupting loadings at a grain terminal in Louisiana.

Three women stripped naked in front of Glickman during his news conference at the Rome summit on Wednesday and accused the United States of ignoring food safety to boost food company profits. They said they were not members of any group.
Environmentalists say they worry that U.S. chemicals group Monsanto Co's Round Up Ready soybean, modified to resist the company's Round Up herbicide, could threaten health.

Dozens of genetically modified products are on the market already, many launched with a minimum of protest. One is Calgene's Flavr-Savr tomato, genetically changed to slow the action of an enzyme that starts the rotting process.
